name: AI Video Creation
objectives: Thinking about videos you watch and make, explain how AI helps with video, what a deepfake is, and the ground rules you will follow, getting at least 3 of 4 right

Given a topic, audience and length, draft a script with AI that has a hook, short scenes and a call to action, and turn it into a storyboard, rewritten in your own voice, with the facts checked and the total time fitting the length
Using a phone, film steady, well-lit shots with clear sound, with permission from everyone on camera and following school filming rules
Using a free video editor, import, trim and order your clips and add a title and call to action as text, following the storyboard with no dead time

Before your video is finished, add accurate captions, music you are allowed to use, and labels for anything AI-generated, with every caption checked and no real person's face or voice made by AI without permission
When the edit is done, get feedback, export the video and share it safely, keeping personal details private and saying how you used AI on school work

lessons.title: Lesson 1: How AI helps with video, and the ground rules
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Name ways AI helps with video and the rules you will follow.
This lesson builds toward: Thinking about videos you watch and make, you will explain how AI helps with video, what a deepfake is, and the ground rules you will follow, getting at least 3 of 4 right.
AI shows up all over video making: assistants that help brainstorm and write scripts, editors that make automatic captions or remove background noise, and generators that create images or clips from a text prompt.
AI can also be misused. A deepfake is a fake video or voice that makes a real person seem to say or do something they did not. Making deepfakes of classmates, teachers or celebrities can hurt people, break school rules and in some places break the law.
Your ground rules: get permission from everyone you film, use only music and clips you are allowed to use, label anything AI-generated, check each app's minimum age, and follow your school's rules.
Words to know:
- Script: the words and actions planned for a video.
- Deepfake: a fake video or voice that makes a real person seem to say or do something they did not.
- AI-generated: made by an AI tool instead of filmed or drawn by a person.
Try it now: Pick the topic of your final video: a club, team, event or cause at your school or in your community. Write one sentence on who the video is for and what you want them to do after watching.
You can now name ways AI helps with video and explain the rules for using it fairly.

check.q: Which of these is a helpful way AI is used in video?
options: Making a fake video of a teacher
Removing background noise from a recording
check.why: AI helps with scripts, captions and noise removal; fakes of real people are misuse.

check.q: A friend wants to make a funny deepfake of the principal for your club video. What do you do?
options: Make it but only show friends
Make it with a blurry face
Say no, because it can hurt people and break rules
check.why: Deepfakes of real people can hurt them, break school rules and in some places break the law.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Writing a script and storyboard with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to draft a short script and turn it into a shot-by-shot storyboard.
This lesson builds toward: Given a topic, audience and length, you will draft a script with AI that has a hook, short scenes and a call to action, and turn it into a storyboard, rewritten in your own voice, with the facts checked and the total time fitting the length.
Short videos need a hook in the first 3 seconds, a clear middle, and an ending that tells people what to do, like "Join us Thursday in Room 12".
Ask AI for a draft: "Write a 45-second script for a video inviting freshmen to join our robotics club. Include a hook, 3 short scenes and a call to action. Use casual words for teens." Then rewrite it so it sounds like you and your club.
A storyboard is the plan for each shot: what we see, what we hear, and how long. Ask AI to turn your script into a table with those columns. You can sketch stick figures too.
Step by step:
- Tell the AI the topic, audience, length and tone.
- Ask for a hook, 3 short scenes and a call to action.
- Rewrite it in your own voice and check the facts (dates, room, times).
- Ask the AI to turn it into a storyboard table: shot, what we see, what we hear, seconds.
- Make sure the total time fits your length.
Words to know:
- Hook: the first few seconds that grab attention.
- Call to action: the line that tells viewers what to do next.
- Storyboard: a shot-by-shot plan of a video.
- Shot: one continuous piece of filming.
Try it now: Use an AI assistant to draft a script for your video topic, rewrite it in your voice, and turn it into a storyboard of 4 to 6 shots that fits your time.
You can now write a short video script and storyboard with help from AI.

options: The plan for each shot: what we see, what we hear and how long
check.why: A storyboard plans each shot before you film.

check.q: AI's script says your club meets in Room 14, but you are not sure. What do you do?
options: Check the room, date and time yourself before filming
Keep it; AI is usually right
Leave the room out of the video
Ask AI if it is sure
check.why: AI can get dates, times or places wrong, so check the facts.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Filming with a phone
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Film steady, well-lit shots with clear sound and permission.
This lesson builds toward: Using a phone, you will film steady, well-lit shots with clear sound, with permission from everyone on camera and following school filming rules.
Light: face the light, like a window, so the light is on the person's face, not behind them. Steady: hold the phone with two hands, lean on something, or use a stand. Turn the phone sideways or keep it tall to match where you will post.
Sound matters more than people think. Film close to the speaker in a quiet place, away from fans and hallways. Record a 3-second test and listen before the real take.
Ask everyone you film if it is OK, and tell them where the video will be shown. Some students cannot be filmed or posted under school rules, so check with your teacher or club advisor. Do not film people in private places or anyone who says no.
Step by step:
- Face the light toward the person.
- Hold the phone steady with two hands or a stand.
- Choose sideways or tall to match where you will post.
- Record a short sound test and listen.
- Get permission from everyone on camera, and follow school filming rules.
Words to know:
- Take: one try at filming a shot.
- Framing: what is inside the edges of the picture.
Try it now: Film the first two shots from your storyboard. Do a sound test first, get permission from anyone on camera, and film each shot at least twice.
You can now film steady, well-lit shots with clear sound, with permission from the people on camera.

check.q: Why record a short sound test before the real take?
options: To hear if the sound is clear before you film
check.why: A 3-second test lets you catch noise or quiet sound before the real take.

check.q: Your club advisor says one student cannot be filmed under school rules. What do you do?
options: Film them and blur it later
Plan the shots so that student is not on camera
check.why: Follow school filming rules and do not film anyone who cannot or does not want to be filmed.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Editing in a free video editor
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Import clips, cut them, put them in order and add text.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free video editor, you will import, trim and order your clips and add a title and call to action as text, following the storyboard with no dead time.
Free editors such as CapCut and Canva work on phones and in web browsers. Menus change often, so look for these actions: start a new project, import or upload your clips, trim (cut the start and end), split a clip, drag clips into order, and add text.
Follow your storyboard. Cut every shot tight: start right before the action and end right after. Dead time makes people scroll away.
Add a title at the start and your call to action as text at the end. Keep text big, short and on screen long enough to read twice.
Step by step:
- Start a new project and import your clips.
- Put the clips in storyboard order.
- Trim the start and end of each clip.
- Add a title and a call to action as text.
- Watch it all the way through and fix anything slow.
Words to know:
- Import: bring your clips into the editor.
- Trim: cut off the start or end of a clip.
- Timeline: the row in the editor where clips sit in order.
Try it now: Import all your shots, put them in storyboard order, trim each one, and add a title and an ending call to action.
You can now edit clips into a tight, ordered video with a title and a call to action.

check.q: What does it mean to cut a shot "tight"?
options: Start right before the action and end right after it
check.why: Tight cuts remove dead time that makes viewers scroll away.

check.q: Your call-to-action text flashes by too fast to read. What do you do?
options: Keep it on screen long enough to read twice
check.why: On-screen text should be big, short and on screen long enough to read twice.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Captions, music and AI visuals, done right
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Add accurate captions, music you may use, and honest labels for AI content.
This lesson builds toward: Before your video is finished, you will add accurate captions, music you are allowed to use, and labels for anything AI-generated, with every caption checked and no real person's face or voice made by AI without permission.
Many people watch with the sound off, and captions help people who are deaf or hard of hearing. Many editors can make automatic captions with AI. Always read them and fix wrong words, especially names.
Music is protected by copyright. According to the U.S. Copyright Office, a work is protected once it is created and fixed, so most songs you hear are protected. Use music from the editor's own library under its rules, music you made, or music with clear permission. Platforms may mute or remove videos that use music without permission.
If you add an AI-generated image or clip, label it, for example "AI-generated image" on screen or in the caption. Never use AI to put a real person's face or voice into your video without their clear permission.
Step by step:
- Turn on automatic captions if your editor has them.
- Read every caption and fix mistakes, especially names.
- Choose music from the editor's library, your own, or with permission.
- Label any AI-generated image or clip.
- Use no real person's face or voice made by AI without permission.
Words to know:
- Captions: words on screen that show what is said.
- Copyright: the legal right of a creator to control copies of their work.
- Label: a short note that says something was made with AI.
Official sources:
- U.S. Copyright Office: Copyright basics FAQ
Try it now: Add captions to your video and fix every mistake. Add music you are allowed to use. If you used any AI-generated image or clip, add a label.
You can now add accurate captions, choose music you may use, and label AI-generated content honestly.

check.q: Why read automatic captions before you publish?
options: AI captions can get words wrong, especially names
check.why: Automatic captions can mishear words, so read and fix them.

check.q: You want a popular song in your club promo. What do you do?
options: Use it and hope no one notices
Use it quietly in the background
Pick music from the editor's library, your own, or with permission
Speed it up so it sounds different
check.why: Most songs are protected; use allowed music or the platform may mute or remove the video.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Reviewing, exporting and sharing safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Get feedback, export your video and share it safely.
This lesson builds toward: When the edit is done, you will get feedback, export the video and share it safely, keeping personal details private and saying how you used AI on school work.
Before you finish, show your video to one or two people and ask: Was the hook strong? Was anything confusing? Did you know what to do at the end? You can also describe your video to an AI assistant and ask for three ways to improve it.
Export the video using the editor's export or save option. Watch the exported file once more to check the sound, captions and ending.
Share it where your club, school and family agree. Keep your full name, school address and schedule out of public posts. If it is a school project, follow your teacher's AI rules and say how you used AI.
Step by step:
- Show the video to one or two people and ask three questions.
- Make one or two improvements.
- Export the video and watch the file once more.
- Share where your club, school and family agree.
- Keep personal details private and say how you used AI on school work.
Words to know:
- Feedback: comments from others that help you improve.
- Export: save your project as a video file.
Try it now: Final task: finish your 30-to-60-second video with AI-helped script and storyboard, at least four shots filmed with permission, captions, music you may use and labels for AI content. Get feedback, export it and share it safely.
You can now plan, film, edit, check and share a short video responsibly with help from AI.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Script and storyboard No hook or call to action, or no storyboard. A script with a hook, scenes and a call to action, in the learner's voice, and a storyboard that fits 30 to 60 seconds. Facts such as dates and rooms are checked, and the storyboard lists seconds per shot. Filming Shots are dark, shaky or hard to hear, or someone was filmed without permission. At least four steady, well-lit shots with clear sound, and permission from everyone on camera. Each shot was filmed at least twice and the best take was chosen. Editing Clips are out of order or have long dead time. Clips follow the storyboard, are trimmed tight, and have a title and an ending call to action. Text is easy to read and the pacing keeps viewers watching. Captions, music and labels Captions have errors, music is not allowed, or AI content is not labeled. Accurate captions, allowed music and a label on anything AI-generated. The learner can say where the music came from and what rules allow it. Feedback and safe sharing Not exported, or shared with personal details. Feedback from at least one person, one change made, exported and shared safely. Notes how AI was used and what changed after feedback. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why watch the exported file once more?
options: To check the sound, captions and ending came out right
check.why: Exports can have problems, so watch the final file before sharing.

check.q: A viewer says they did not know what to do at the end. What do you change?
options: Make the call to action clearer
check.why: Feedback about the ending means the call to action needs to be clearer.
